content: Bishop Auckland General Hospital is a relatively small but highly modern NHS district general hospital. The majority of its catchment area is rural. The hospital was inaugurated in 2002, initially with approximately 286 beds, although the number of beds fluctuates over time. There has been significant controversy surrounding the recent reduction in services at this hospital. It is part of the County Durham and Darlington Foundation Trust. A major point of contention has been the closure of the Special Care Baby Unit (SCBU). Neonates requiring specialized care are now transferred to Darlington Memorial Hospital. Additionally, Ward 3, which was dedicated to haematology, has been shut down. The number of surgical beds has been significantly reduced, and the hospital now primarily performs minor surgical procedures, many of which are conducted as day cases. Despite these changes, the overall quality and utilization of services within the County Durham and Darlington Foundation Trust have been rated as good by the Healthcare Commission. The trust's other two main facilities are Darlington Memorial Hospital and the University Hospital of North Durham. Bishop Auckland General Hospital continues to operate an Accident & Emergency (A&E) department. It also performs elective surgeries and day surgeries. The hospital offers a range of acute medical specialties, including diabetology, endocrinology, cardiology, and respiratory medicine. It houses a Critical Care Unit, which includes both Intensive Therapy Unit (ITU) and Coronary Care Unit (CCU) beds. The hospital provides general rehabilitation care for inpatients. It also features a dedicated stroke unit, a rehabilitation daycare centre, and a chemotherapy day unit.
